lesson_1.title: Creating Your First List
task: Lists are a great way to group related items together. Think of a list like a row of lockers where you can put numbers or text. Let's practice making one from scratch.
1. Open the 'Functions' tab and make a function named `create_basic_array`.
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and drag out the 'create list with' block.
3. Click the gear icon on the list block to make sure it has exactly 3 item slots.
4. Grab number blocks from the 'Math' tab and put `10`, `20`, and `30` into the slots.

lesson_1.title: Finding the List Length
task: Often, you need to know exactly how many items are inside a list. Programming makes this super easy with a 'length of' block.
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and find the 'length of' block.
3. Snap your `arr` variable into the 'length of' block.

lesson_1.title: Getting the First Item
task: In programming, we count list positions (called 'indices') starting from 0. So, the very first item is always at index 0.
2. First, we need to be safe: use an 'If' block from the 'Logic' tab to check if the list is empty using the 'is empty' block from the Lists tab. If it is, return `0`.
3. If it's not empty, open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'in list get' block.
4. Set it to get the item at index 0 from `arr`.

lesson_1.title: Changing Items in a List
task: You can swap out an item in a list without deleting the whole list. You just tell the computer which spot to update and give it a new value.
2. Check if the list is empty. If it is, return the list as it is.
3. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'in list set' block.
4. Tell it to set the item at index 0 to the number `99`.

lesson_1.title: Adding Items to the End
task: Lists are flexible. You can always add new things to the end of a list. In programming, this action is called 'appending'.
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'append to list' block.
3. Attach your `item` variable and your `arr` variable to the block.

lesson_2.title: Adding Up a List
task: To look at every single item in a list, we use a loop. Let's practice by walking through a list and adding all the numbers together.
2. Go to the 'Variables' tab and create a variable called `total`. Set it to 0.
3. Open the 'Loops' tab and drag out the 'for each item in list' block. Attach `arr` to it.
4. Inside the loop, go to the 'Math' tab and grab the modify variable block (e.g., `item += 1`). Set it to add the current loop item to your `total`.

lesson_2.title: Finding the Biggest Number
task: To find the biggest item, we can loop through the list and keep track of the largest number we've seen so far.
2. Create a variable called `max_val` and set it to the first item (`arr[0]`).
3. Use a 'for each item' loop to look at every number in the list.
4. Use an 'If' block: if the current item is greater than `max_val`, use a 'set' block to update `max_val` to the current item.

lesson_2.title: Counting Specific Items (Evens)
task: Sometimes you only want to count items that match a certain rule. Let's loop through a list and count how many even numbers are inside.
3. Start a 'for each item' loop for the list.
4. Inside the loop, check if the number is even using the modulo block from the 'Math' tab (`item % 2 == 0`).
5. If it is even, add 1 to `count`.

lesson_2.title: Does the List Have This Number?
task: How do you find out if a specific number is in a messy list? You check every spot until you see it!
2. Use a 'for each item' loop to check every number in the list.
3. Inside the loop, use an 'If' block to check if the current item equals the `target`.
4. If it matches, immediately use the 'return' block to return `True`.
5. If the loop finishes and you didn't find it, return `False` at the bottom of the function.

lesson_2.title: Copying a List
task: Let's practice making a brand new list by copying everything from an old list, item by item.
2. Create a new empty list called `result` from the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab.
3. Use a 'for each item' loop to look at every item in `arr`.
4. Inside the loop, use the 'append' block to add the current item to `result`.

lesson_3.title: Removing the Last Item
task: Lists have lots of built-in tools. Instead of writing complex code, you can use built-in blocks to do heavy lifting. Let's 'pop' an item!
2. Check if the list is empty. If so, return `'Empty'`.
3. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'remove and get last item from list' block.
4. Return the result of that block.

lesson_3.title: Removing a Specific Value
task: What if you want to delete a specific word or number, but you don't know where it is? The 'remove first occurrence' block handles this for you.
2. Open the 'Logic' tab and use an 'If' block to check if the `target` is in the list using the `is in` block.
3. If it is in the list, go to the 'Lists' tab and use the 'remove first occurrence of' block to delete it from `arr`.

lesson_3.title: Checking if a List is Empty
task: We have been checking length manually, but there is a dedicated tool just for this!
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'is list empty' block.

lesson_3.title: Counting Occurrences Quickly
task: Earlier, we built a loop to count items. Programming languages give us a built-in 'count' block to do this instantly without writing a loop!
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and find the 'count occurrences of' block.

lesson_3.title: Sorting a List
task: Sorting means putting items in order from smallest to biggest. Doing this manually is hard, but using the built-in sort block makes it easy!
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'sort list' block.

lesson_4.title: Combining Two Lists
task: Sometimes you have two separate lists, and you just want to stick them together into one long list.
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and find the 'join list and list' block.
3. Snap your two lists into the block.

lesson_4.title: Keeping Only Positive Numbers
task: Let's clean up a messy list by creating a brand new list that only keeps the positive numbers (numbers greater than 0).
2. Create a new empty list called `result`.
3. Loop through `arr` using the 'for each item' loop.
4. If a number is `> 0`, append it to your `result` list.

lesson_4.title: Is the List in Order?
task: To check if a list is perfectly sorted from smallest to biggest, we just have to look at neighbors. If we ever see a big number sitting to the left of a smaller number, it's not sorted!
2. Open the 'Loops' tab and use a 'count with i' loop. Set it to count from 0 to length of arr minus 1.
3. Inside the loop, check if `arr[i]` is strictly greater than `arr[i+1]`.
5. If the loop finishes without finding any bad neighbors, return `True`.

lesson_4.title: Slicing a List
task: Slicing means chopping out a specific middle section of a list to create a smaller list.
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'slice list' block.
3. Set the start index to `1` and the end index to `3`.

lesson_4.title: Inserting an Item
task: You don't always have to add items to the very end of a list. You can squeeze them in anywhere using 'insert'!
2. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and find the 'insert at index' block.
3. Tell it to insert your `item` variable at index `0` into the `arr` list.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Reversing In-Place
task: Our old reverse list task required us to build a completely brand new list, which takes up extra memory! Let's do it faster by just swapping the items in the list we already have.
2. Create two trackers (pointers). Make `left` start at 0, and `right` start at the very last index of the list (`length - 1`).
3. Open the 'Loops' tab and make a `while` loop that runs as long as `left < right`.
4. Inside the loop, use your custom 'swap variable' block (or manually swap them) to swap `arr[left]` with `arr[right]`.
5. Add 1 to `left` and subtract 1 from `right` so they move closer to the middle.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Max and Min Together
task: If you want to find BOTH the biggest and the smallest number in a list, you don't need to loop through the list twice. You can do it all in one single loop to save time!
1. Set both `max_val` and `min_val` to the first item in the list.
2. Make a single 'for each item' loop to look at every item in the list.
3. Inside the loop, if the item is bigger than `max_val`, update `max_val`. Also, if the item is smaller than `min_val`, update `min_val`!
4. Create a list block and put `min_val` in the first slot and `max_val` in the second slot, then return it.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Quick Cleanup (Sets)
task: In programming, a 'Set' is a special container that is not allowed to have any duplicate items. If you put a messy list into a Set, it instantly cleans out all the duplicates for you!
1. Delete any slow loops you have that check for duplicates.
2. Open the 'Sets & Tuples' tab and grab the 'create set from list' block. Apply it to your list.
3. Open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'create list from' block. Apply it to your Set to turn it back into a list.
4. Return the new, clean list. It's much faster than checking items one by one!
